title: Business Factor Analysis
description: Analyze how a real business combines all four factors of production by calculating factor payments (rent, wages, interest) and determining entrepreneurial profit or loss based on realistic business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Calculate monthly factor payments for land (rent), labor (wages), and capital (interest)
Determine entrepreneurial profit by subtracting all costs from revenue
Understand profit margin as a measure of business viability
Analyze which factors cost the most for different business types
instructions: Select one of four business types to analyze: Coffee Shop, Tech Startup, Family Farm, or Construction Company
Read the business description and hints about typical costs in each category
Enter estimated monthly factor payments: rent (land), wages (labor), interest (capital), and other costs
Enter estimated monthly revenue based on the business model
Calculate profit to see if the business is viable and view profit margin analysis
Answer reflection questions about which factor is most expensive and how to increase profit
materials_needed: Business scenario descriptions with cost hints

business_scenarios.name: Downtown Coffee Shop
business_scenarios.description: A cozy coffee shop in {{STATE_NAME}}'s downtown area serving espresso drinks, pastries, and light breakfast.

hints.labor: 1 manager + 3 baristas (~8 hours/day). Consider {{STATE_MIN_WAGE}} minimum wage.
hints.capital: Espresso machine ($15,000), grinder ($2,000), POS system ($1,500), furniture ($5,000). Loan at 7% interest.

business_scenarios.name: Software Startup
business_scenarios.description: A small tech company building a mobile app for local service providers in {{STATE_NAME}}.

hints.labor: 2 developers ($70k each), 1 designer ($50k), founder (deferred). Calculate monthly.
hints.capital: Computers ($10,000), software licenses ($500/month), servers ($200/month). Minimal loan needed.

typical_answer_range.note: Negative profit is common for startups in growth phase

business_scenarios.name: Family Farm Operation
business_scenarios.description: A 200-acre farm in {{STATE_NAME}} growing crops and selling at farmers markets.

hints.land: 200 acres: land value ~$5,000/acre, annual property tax ~$2,000, or rent ~$200/acre/year
hints.labor: Family labor (2 full-time equivalent) + seasonal workers (3 months)
hints.capital: Tractor ($50,000), implements ($30,000), irrigation ($20,000). Loan at 6% interest.
hints.revenue: Crop yield varies. Estimate $400/acre gross for mixed vegetables.

rent.calculation: If owned: property tax $2,000/year ÷ 12. If rented: 200 acres × $200/acre ÷ 12

typical_answer_range.note: Farms often have seasonal income concentrated in harvest months

business_scenarios.name: Construction Company
business_scenarios.description: A residential construction company in {{STATE_NAME}} building custom homes.

hints.land: Office/yard space: ~$3,000/month. Job sites are customer-owned.
hints.labor: Project manager ($60k), 5 skilled workers ($45k each), admin ($35k)
hints.capital: Trucks ($80,000), tools/equipment ($50,000), office equipment ($10,000). Loan at 7%.
hints.other: Materials vary by project, insurance, permits (~$20,000/month average)
hints.revenue: 2-3 homes/year at $50,000 profit margin each. Monthly varies greatly.

loss.message: This business is operating at a loss. The entrepreneur would lose money each month. Consider reducing costs or increasing revenue.

thin_margin.message: Thin margins! Profit is low relative to revenue. One bad month could wipe out profits.

reasonable.message: Reasonable profit. This is typical for many small businesses.

strong.message: Excellent profit margin! This business model looks very strong.

reflection_questions.question: Which factor is most expensive for this business?

typical_answers.farm: Capital and other costs (equipment, inputs) are largest
typical_answers.construction: Labor is largest, followed by materials (other)

reflection_questions.question: How could the entrepreneur increase profit?
example_answers: Increase revenue (raise prices, increase volume, add services)
Reduce labor costs (automation, efficiency, better training)
Reduce rent (relocate, negotiate lease, share space)
Reduce capital costs (buy used equipment, lease instead of own)
Improve efficiency (reduce waste, better inventory management)

deliverables: Completed factor payment calculations for chosen business
Calculated profit or loss and profit margin percentage
Visual breakdown of costs using pie chart
Analysis of which factor is most expensive

criteria: Correctly calculated all factor payments within reasonable ranges
Accurately determined profit by subtracting total costs from revenue
Understood profit margin interpretation and business viability
Identified cost drivers and proposed reasonable improvement strategies

teacher_notes: Students often underestimate labor costs and overestimate profit margins. Real businesses typically operate on 5-15% profit margins, not 50%+. The Tech Startup intentionally shows negative profit to illustrate that startups often lose money while building their customer base. Use this to discuss cash flow challenges and why entrepreneurs need capital reserves. The interactive calculator helps students see how small changes in costs or revenue dramatically impact profitability.
